churches_of_christ.faith_and_works:
Members of Churches of Christ teach that salvation is by God's grace and cannot be earned. They also speak of obedient faith: a faith that responds to God by repenting, confessing Jesus as Lord and being baptized. These steps are not understood as payments or good works that earn salvation, but as the way a believer accepts the gift.

Because of this, Churches of Christ are often careful to say that they do not teach salvation by works. Baptism in particular is regarded as an act of faith in which God works, not as a human accomplishment. They differ from traditions which stress faith alone as an inward act, and from those which regard baptism as an optional sign following salvation. Within Churches of Christ there are varying emphases about how to explain the relationship.
churches_of_christ.one_true_church:
Members of Churches of Christ speak of the church of Christ, using a biblical name, to mean the body of all who belong to Christ and follow the New Testament pattern. Many say that they wish to be Christians only, not a denomination, and they avoid denominational titles and creeds.

Historically, some in this tradition taught that only members of Churches of Christ were truly saved, and this view is still held by some. Many others today say that God alone knows who belongs to him, and that Christians exist in many fellowships. They continue to hold that the New Testament pattern for the church is worth following. Most other Christians hear the name as a claim to exclusivity, and members often address this directly.
churches_of_christ.local_church:
In Churches of Christ, the local congregation is the whole of the church at that place, and it governs itself. There is no denominational headquarters, synod or governing body over the congregations. Each is led by a group of elders, sometimes called shepherds or overseers, who are chosen by the congregation, and served by deacons and often a preaching minister who is hired by the local church.

Congregations cooperate freely in mission work, in schools and in benevolent ministries, but these are voluntary arrangements and do not rule the churches. The conviction behind this is that the New Testament shows independent local churches led by their own elders, so no structure beyond the local church has authority. This means that practice can differ somewhat from one congregation to another.
churches_of_christ.restoration:
Churches of Christ trace their heritage to the Restoration Movement, or Stone-Campbell Movement, which arose in the early nineteenth century in the United States. Its aim was to restore the church to the pattern of the New Testament, and by doing so to overcome the divisions of Christianity.

Members set aside human creeds and denominational names, and try to rely on the Bible alone for their teaching and practice, asking what the earliest churches believed and did. They hope this can lead to Christian unity based on Scripture. They recognize that the movement itself divided into several branches, and members differ over how successfully the ideal has been carried out. The word restoration expresses the aim of going back to the source, not a claim of perfection.
churches_of_christ.baptism:
Churches of Christ teach that baptism is immersion of a believer in water for the forgiveness of sins, drawing especially on the passage in the Acts of the Apostles where Peter tells the crowd to repent and be baptized. Together with faith, repentance and confession of Christ, baptism is understood as part of how a person responds to the gospel.

Members stress that the water has no power of its own and that it is God who forgives when a person in faith is baptized. They do not consider infant baptism or sprinkling to be baptism, since a baby cannot believe and the word means immersion. This differs from traditions that regard baptism only as a sign of forgiveness already received, and members are used to explaining why they see it differently.
churches_of_christ.instrumental_music:
Most Churches of Christ worship a cappella, meaning that the congregation sings without instruments. They point out that the New Testament commands and describes singing in worship but does not mention instruments in the assemblies of the early church, and that the church historically sang unaccompanied for centuries.

The conviction is that where Scripture is silent, the church should be careful not to add to what God has commanded. Worship is meant to be pure singing from the heart, with every voice taking part. Members generally do not regard people who use instruments as unbelievers, but consider unaccompanied singing to be the faithful pattern. Some congregations, and some members, have raised questions about the practice, and a few now use instruments.
